## Week 6: Retrieval and Ranking Architectures

```{=html}
<div class="cp-frame-bg cp-frame-navy"></div>
<div class="cp-frame-content">
  <div class="cp-frame-label" style="background:#003D7C;color:#EF7C00;">WEEK 06 · IR AND RAG SYSTEMS</div>
  <div class="cp-frame-title cp-text--navy">From a corpus to a defensible context</div>
  <div class="cp-frame-body" style="color:#333;">
    <p style="margin:0 0 .65em;">This week treats retrieval as a <strong>multi-stage systems problem</strong>: preserve useful evidence early, then spend expensive computation only where it can change the final answer.</p>
    <div class="cp-grid cp-grid--2" style="align-items:stretch;">
      <div class="cp-card cp-card--soft"><span class="cp-kicker">System reasoning</span><p class="cp-card__title">Trace the cascade</p><p class="cp-card__meta">Explain the distinct jobs of retrieval, ranking, re-ranking, and context assembly.</p></div>
      <div class="cp-card cp-card--soft"><span class="cp-kicker">Complexity reasoning</span><p class="cp-card__title">Budget the work</p><p class="cp-card__meta">Reason about runtime, memory, candidate depth, embedding dimension, and token budget.</p></div>
      <div class="cp-card cp-card--soft"><span class="cp-kicker">Architecture reasoning</span><p class="cp-card__title">Design the hand-offs</p><p class="cp-card__meta">Choose what an index, a lightweight ranker, and a deep re-ranker should each know.</p></div>
      <div class="cp-card cp-card--warning"><span class="cp-kicker">Stakeholder reasoning</span><p class="cp-card__title">Audit what is lost</p><p class="cp-card__meta">Evaluate recall, provenance, visibility, and source diversity—not only a final relevance score.</p></div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: notes
Delivery: 2 minutes. State the outcomes as design capabilities rather than a list to memorise. Connect the prior exercise to the first hand-off: current-session signals may be valuable, but they must be available and affordable at the stage where they are used. Preview the notation used today: corpus size N, candidate depths K1, K2, and K3, embedding dimension d, joint sequence length L, and context token budget B.
:::

## Why retrieval alone cannot choose the final evidence

```{=html}
<div class="cp-stack" style="max-width:92%;margin:0 auto;">
  <p style="margin:0;color:#425466;font-size:.88em;">Each stage receives fewer items and is allowed to use more expensive evidence. A document removed early cannot be recovered later.</p>
  <div style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:1fr .14fr 1fr .14fr 1fr .14fr 1fr;align-items:stretch;gap:.32em;">
    <div class="cp-flow-card"><span class="cp-kicker">Indexed retrieval</span><strong>Corpus N</strong><span class="cp-card__meta">Sparse, dense, or hybrid search</span></div>
    <div class="cp-flow-arrow" aria-hidden="true">→</div>
    <div class="cp-flow-card"><span class="cp-kicker">Candidate set</span><strong>K₁ ≈ 1,000</strong><span class="cp-card__meta">High recall under a latency budget</span></div>
    <div class="cp-flow-arrow" aria-hidden="true">→</div>
    <div class="cp-flow-card"><span class="cp-kicker">Lightweight ranking</span><strong>K₂ ≈ 100</strong><span class="cp-card__meta">Richer request-time features</span></div>
    <div class="cp-flow-arrow" aria-hidden="true">→</div>
    <div class="cp-flow-card"><span class="cp-kicker">Deep re-ranking</span><strong>K₃ ≈ 10–30</strong><span class="cp-card__meta">Joint query-document relevance</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="cp-card cp-card--prompt" style="margin-top:.25em;"><strong>Then assemble:</strong> deduplicate, diversify, preserve provenance, and fit evidence within the RAG context budget <strong>B</strong>.</div>
</div>
```

::: notes
Delivery: 3 minutes. Retrieval is deliberately broad: it should retain plausible evidence, not make the final semantic distinction. The lightweight ranker makes a first precision-oriented cut with features that are more expensive or less indexable than retrieval features. The deep re-ranker reads query and document together, so it is reserved for a shortlist. Context assembly is not another relevance model: it is a list-level and token-budget decision. Ask: “If a relevant source falls outside K1, can a perfect re-ranker rescue it?” No.
:::

## Why not use one deep scoring stage? {background-color="#ffffff"}

```{=html}
<div class="cp-grid cp-grid--2" style="align-items:stretch;">
  <div class="cp-card cp-card--warning">
    <span class="cp-kicker">Single-stage deep scoring</span>
    <p class="cp-card__title">Apply joint attention to every retrieved candidate</p>
    <p style="margin:.45em 0;"><strong>Input:</strong> K₁ candidates, each with a query-document sequence of length L.</p>
    <div class="cp-metric cp-metric--orange"><span class="cp-metric__label">Approximate attention compute</span><span class="cp-metric__value">O(K₁L²d)</span><span class="cp-metric__meta">K₁ candidates × quadratic sequence interaction × hidden dimension d</span></div>
    <p class="cp-card__meta" style="margin-top:.6em;">With K₁ = 1,000, every request fetches and jointly processes 1,000 document texts. The most expensive model is spent on many weak candidates.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="cp-card cp-card--soft">
    <span class="cp-kicker">Staged ranking and re-ranking</span>
    <p class="cp-card__title">Use deep joint scoring only after two cheaper cuts</p>
    <div class="cp-stack" style="gap:.35em;">
      <div><strong>Retrieve:</strong> N → K₁ with an index; exact dense scan is O(Nd), while ANN trades exactness for measured speed.</div>
      <div><strong>Rank:</strong> K₁ → K₂ with lightweight features, often O(K₁d) or a bounded feature-model cost.</div>
      <div><strong>Re-rank:</strong> K₂ → K₃ with joint attention, O(K₂L²d).</div>
    </div>
    <div class="cp-metric"><span class="cp-metric__label">Deep-scoring reduction</span><span class="cp-metric__value">K₁ / K₂</span><span class="cp-metric__meta">1,000 → 20 means 50× fewer joint query-document evaluations</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: notes
Delivery: 3 minutes. Contrast the columns carefully. The left is not merely slow because it has many candidates; self-attention makes each query-document comparison much more expensive than a cached-vector score. The right column does not claim a universal ANN complexity bound: latency and recall depend on index type, hardware, and configuration. The engineering claim is that stages reserve expensive query-document interaction for candidates that survived cheaper evidence. The next sections make these terms concrete with index, embedding, and ranking code.
:::

# ☕ When Google results danced {background-color="#000000"}

```{=html}
<div class="cp-grid cp-grid--2" style="min-height:62vh;align-items:center;color:#fff;">
  <div class="cp-stack" style="display:flex;min-height:58vh;flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;">

      <div class="cp-kicker cp-text--orange" style="margin-bottom:.7em;">While you pause · a search-history aside</div>
      <p style="margin:0;max-width:28em;color:#d8d8d8;font-size:1.02em;line-height:1.4;">In 2003, the <em>Google Dance</em> described a monthly index update. For several days, searches could alternate between old and new index versions—so rankings appeared to move.</p>
      <p style="margin:.7em 0 0;font-size:.68em;line-height:1.35;"><a href="https://www.webmoves.net/2003/07/19/google-dance-the-index-update-of-the-google-search-engine/" target="_blank" rel="noopener" style="color:#f6b56b;text-decoration:underline;">Read the contemporaneous 2003 account ↗</a></p>
```
